portal_hypertension.abstract: Identifying patients with advanced fibrosis and portal hypertension is a crucial component of risk stratifying patients with liver disease. The reference standard is liver biopsy for detection of fibrosis and cirrhosis and measurement of hepatic venous pressure gradient for detection of portal hypertension. However, many noninvasive blood-based and imaging-based assessments have been developed and studied over the years. We review the most commonly available and accessible ones in the ultrasound. We also review 2 simplified algorithms that integrate blood-based and imaging-based tools in detecting advanced fibrosis and clinically significant portal hypertension.

portal_hypertension.abstract: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a major complication of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). Stent under-dilation reduces HE, but a fixed diameter cannot be individualised to patient risk. An individualised scoring system tailoring balloon diameter to patient characteristics, without compromising efficacy or increasing variceal re-bleeding or stent dysfunction, is needed. In this retrospective study, 717 patients with cirrhosis underwent TIPS with 8-mm covered stents between December 2015 and December 2023. portal_hypertension.abstract: Minimally invasive liver resection is increasingly performed, even in patients with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension. However, the benefits of robotic liver resection over laparoscopic liver resection in patients with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension remain unclear. We conducted a post hoc international, multicenter study including 2,328 patients with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension who underwent minimally invasive liver resection (2,004 laparoscopic liver resection and 324 robotic liver resection). portal_hypertension.abstract: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is an immune-mediated liver disease in which persistent necroinflammation drives progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and ultimately portal hypertension-related decompensation. Effective immunosuppression may halt hepatic inflammation, thereby inducing biochemical (and histological) remission, facilitating regeneration of hepatic function, clinical recompensation, and fibrosis regression. Studies indicate that approximately 19-54% of immunosuppressed patients achieve recompensation. This retrospective study included 454 cirrhotic patients from center A and 77 from center B. CSPH labels were available only for patients from center A.
